component_findings.async_structured: Recertified level 4 under the current criterion: Asynchronous concurrency has first-class composition and structured lifetime/join/cancellation mechanisms or an equivalent disciplined model. Evidence basis: Swift's concurrency design (structured concurrency + actors + compile-time Sendable/data-race checking) is one of the more advanced and safety-oriented concurrency designs among mainstream languages, comparable in ambition to Rust's ownership-based concurrency safety but achieved with less ceremony, though the ecosystem-wide transition to strict concurrency is still incomplete (an ecosystem/maturity concern excluded here). | Swift | Swift has a modern, language-integrated structured concurrency model (async/await, Task, TaskGroup, AsyncSequence) introduced in Swift 5.5, built into the compiler and standard library rather than bolted on as a library. | Actors provide a language-level data-race-avoidance primitive: actor-isolated state is checked at compile time, preventing many classes of shared-mutable-state races without runtime locks in common cases. | Sendable checking and strict concurrency checking (progressively enforced, mandatory by default in Swift 6 language mode) give compile-time diagnostics for data races crossing concurrency domains, a significant safety-oriented differentiator versus most mainstream languages. | Structured concurrency (child tasks scoped to parent task lifetime, automatic cancellation propagation) reduces common resource-leak and orphan-task bugs compared to unstructured thread/callback models. | Global actors (e.g. @MainActor) provide ergonomic…

component_findings.abi_calling_control: Recertified level 4 under the current criterion: ABI/calling-convention/linkage choices are explicit or safely standardized for common interoperability cases. Evidence basis: Swift's FFI design is strong for C and Objective-C (module-based automatic import, no manual header duplication) and increasingly strong for C++ via native C++ interop, which is more ergonomic than most competitors' C++ bridging (which typically requires C wrapper shims). It lacks a general foreign-function story beyond the C-family ABI, same limitation shared by nearly every non-JVM/CLR language, so it is rated above average but not top-tier (no universal multi-language interop layer like JVM/CLR based languages). | Swift | Swift has first-class, low-friction C interop via automatic ClangImporter bridging: C headers/modules are imported directly as Swift declarations without manual glue code, and Swift can be exposed to C/Objective-C via @objc and generated headers. | C++ interop (Swift/C++ interoperability, stabilized in Swift 5.9+) allows importing C++ types/functions directly with automatic bridging of value types, templates (partial), and STL containers, though template/generic C++ code and complex ABI cases remain limited. | Interop with non-C-family languages (Rust, Go, etc.) requires going through a C ABI boundary (C shims), same as most native languages; no direct native bridge exists. | Objective-C interop is exceptionally mature (bidirectional, near-seamless) reflecting the platform heritage, but this is Apple-platform-specific rather than a general FFI story. | On L…
